lesson.title: Counting Genes: How to Measure Allele Frequency
lesson.summary: Allele frequency is the proportion of all gene copies at a locus in a population that are a particular allele, a value calculated directly from genotype counts and the fundamental quantity population geneticists track to detect evolutionary change.
lesson.body:
An allele frequency is simply a proportion: out of every copy of a particular gene present in a population's gene pool, what fraction are a specific allele? It is a single number, usually expressed as a decimal between 0 and 1, or as a percentage, that summarizes how common one version of a gene is relative to the other versions in circulation.

Calculating an allele frequency directly from a population is a straightforward counting exercise, and working through the arithmetic makes the concept concrete. Consider an autosomal gene with two alleles, A and a, in a population of 100 individuals. Because this is a diploid, biparental population, each individual carries two allele copies at this locus, so there are 200 total allele copies in the population's gene pool at this gene. Suppose a genetic survey finds the following genotype counts: 49 individuals are AA, 42 are Aa, and 9 are aa. As a check, 49 plus 42 plus 9 equals 100 individuals, confirming the counts are consistent.

To get the allele frequencies, count actual allele copies, not individuals. Every AA individual contributes two A alleles, and every Aa individual contributes one A allele, since the other copy in each heterozygote is a. So the total count of A alleles is 2 times 49, plus 42, which is 98 plus 42, equaling 140. Similarly, every aa individual contributes two a alleles, and every Aa individual contributes one a allele, giving 2 times 9, plus 42, which is 18 plus 42, equaling 60. As a check, 140 A alleles plus 60 a alleles equals 200, matching the total allele count expected from 100 diploid individuals. Dividing each count by the total gives the frequencies. The frequency of A, conventionally written p, is 140 divided by 200, equaling 0.70. The frequency of a, conventionally written q, is 60 divided by 200, equaling 0.30. As a final check, p plus q equals 0.70 plus 0.30, which is 1.00, a relationship that will always hold true when there are only two alleles at a locus, since together they account for every copy of that gene in the population.

Notice what this calculation did and did not assume. It used only the actual, observed genotype counts, individuals directly counted by their genotype, with no assumption about how those genotypes came to be distributed the way they are. That is an important distinction to hold onto going into the next chapter: calculating an allele frequency this way is a direct empirical measurement, while the Hardy-Weinberg model covered next runs a related calculation in the opposite direction, starting from allele frequencies and predicting what genotype frequencies should look like under a specific, idealized set of assumptions. Comparing that prediction to real, directly measured genotype counts like the ones above is exactly how biologists use the Hardy-Weinberg model to detect whether a population is evolving.

Allele frequencies are the quantity population genetics ultimately cares about tracking over time, since a change in allele frequency across generations is, by the definition introduced in the last chapter, evolution happening. Frequencies can shift for several reasons: new mutations introducing new alleles, migration moving alleles between populations, chance effects in small populations, non-random mating, and natural selection favoring some alleles over others, each explored in more depth elsewhere in this course. The tool for telling whether frequencies are shifting at all, and the essential first step before asking why, is the Hardy-Weinberg model covered next.
